Customer wants a 4-week pilot to validate p95 latency and per-token cost for a hybrid hosted/dedicated setup; important constraints include strict VPC networking, SOC2 compliance, and a hard monthly budget. transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-15 16:00 UTC | Duration: 54m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Rodriguez (Redwood SE), Anya Patel (Redwood SE), Rajiv Patel (Opalware CTO), Emma Stone (Head of ML), Caroline Vega (SRE), Ben Holmes (Product)
Links shared: POC template deck (redwood.com/s/poctemplate), cost model spreadsheet (sheetly.link/opalware-cost), benchmark scripts (github.com/redwood/bench-kits)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya, AE on this account. Quick round-robin then we'll dive into econ and the bench plan.
[00:18] Rajiv: Hi all, Rajiv here. We run the core recommendation and search stack, want to evaluate LLMinf for personalized snippets and re-rank. Budget is tight, so this is mostly about unit cost and tail latency.
[00:31] Emma: Hi, Emma — ML lead. We want to know: can we get p95 < 150ms for short prompts (~80 tokens) and keep cost under our internal target.
[00:45] Caroline: Caroline — SRE. Big ask: VPC-only, SAML SSO, audit logs and KMS integration. Not comfortable pushing data outside our VPC for now.
[00:58] Liam: Thanks. We'll scope a pilot that can run in Private (VPC) or Dedicated depending on network constraints; for cost modeling we usually show hosted vs dedicated delta. Quick Q: what's your expected steady RPS and peak burst?
[01:12] Ben: Steady around 80 RPS, peak up to 250 for launches. Concurrency we think about 40-60 active requests.
[01:30] Maya: Good, that's helpful. For econ we need average prompt length and average response length, and distribution. Emma, can you share sample prompts?
[01:39] Emma: Yep, will share 500 prompts. Avg input 60 tokens, output ~40 tokens. There's a long-tail of long queries — maybe 5% > 512 tokens.
[01:50] Liam: Okay. For the benchmark plan we recommended two vectors: synthetic replay (from your logs) and a generative set to stress longer sequences. We'll test two model configs: baseline FP16 variant and an int8 quant variant to show cost/loss tradeoff.
[02:05] Rajiv: How do you show the per-token cost? We want a simple number to plug into our TCO model.
[02:12] Anya: We'll give per-1k token estimates and a per-call average. Example numbers for similar profiles: hosted FP16 ~ $0.65 per 1k tokens, hosted int8 ~ $0.22 per 1k tokens after batching/caching; dedicated reserved capacity can drop effective cost by 20-40% depending on commit. These are ballpark until we run the bench.
[02:33] Ben: Those ranges are huge — what's driving the difference?
[02:37] Liam: Two main levers: batching and prefix/KV caching. If your prompts repeat prefixes (e.g., user profile context), KV caching can cut token work dramatically. Also model variant/quantization changes per-token ops. Finally, utilization of GPU and tail latency SLO influences effective cost — low utilization means higher unit cost.
[02:56] Emma: In our logs, around 30% of requests include identical user profile prefixes. Could be big win.
[03:05] Caroline: But caching in a strict VPC private deploy, is that supported?
[03:09] Liam: Yes, caching and KV store run alongside the inference runtime in Private. We'll need networking rules for shared caches between pods if you scale horizontally; we can propose an architecture in the SOW.
[03:22] Maya: Let's define success criteria now — Rajiv?
[03:27] Rajiv: Primary: p95 latency for 80-token responses <= 150ms; Secondary: cost per 1M tokens delivered <= $600 (i.e., approx $0.60 per 1k tokens) and no PII leaving the VPC. Also HIPAA/SOC2 compliance checklist for audit.
[03:45] Liam: Noted. We'll include those target metrics in the SLO section.
[03:50] Anya: For bench measurements we'll capture p50/p95/p99, throughput curves, GPU util, and per-call byte token breakdown. We'll also run a canary with burst to 250 RPS.
[04:05] Emma: Timeline? We want results asap.
[04:08] Maya: Proposed 4-week pilot: week 0-1 prep and infra + SSO/KMS connectivity, week 2 bench runs and tuning, week 3 validation and quality checks, week 4 wrap-up and recommendations. If networking slows us, infra could extend by a week.
[04:26] Rajiv: Who'll need to be involved from our side?
[04:29] Maya: Short list: an infra/SRE engineer for VPC and KMS (Caroline), an ML engineer to validate quality tradeoffs (Emma), and a product owner for acceptance (Ben). Redwood will provide SE time (Liam/Anya) and an infra engineer for deployment support.
[04:45] Ben: On quality: how do we measure generation quality drop with int8?
[04:49] Liam: We'll run eval sets and automated metrics (BLEU/EM/MD5-ish nucleotide — joke) and human review for a sample. For int8 we usually see small degradation on some tasks; we report query-level deltas and have rollback configs.
[05:05] Rajiv: Are there any lock-in or migration concerns if we do Dedicated?
[05:09] Maya: The API and config are consistent across Hosted/Dedicated/Private — you can switch models and rollbacks without re-writing app logic. Dedicated is reserved capacity on our infra, with commit discounts. Private is customer-managed network; portability depends on your infra but we provide a packaging and helm chart for on-prem.
[05:28] Emma: For the cost model, can you show sensitivity to batching? Like 1 request per batch vs 8 vs 32?
[05:33] Anya: Yes. We'll include a table: per-1k cost as function of average batch size and cache hit rate. Rough example: FP16 at batch=1 $0.85/1k, batch=8 $0.40/1k, batch=32 $0.28/1k. Int8 at batch=8 can go as low as $0.18/1k in some configs. Again, approximate until benched.
[05:56] Caroline: What's the risk of failures during the pilot? We need fallbacks.
[06:00] Liam: We'll propose a fallback policy: route to a smaller base model if the primary model misses SLOs, and automatic throttling under overload. We'll also push logs to your SIEM via secure forwarder.
[06:12] Rajiv: What about security artifacts — do you have an SOC2 pack and KMS integration docs?
[06:16] Maya: Yes. I'll attach security docs in the follow-up: SOC2 report, architecture with KMS/HSM, SAML SSO guide, and network requirements.
[06:24] Ben: Bench specifics: can you replicate tokenization differences? Our tokenizer is slightly different from the reference one you use.
[06:29] Liam: Bring your tokenizer or we can run inside the bench harness to match exactly. Tokenization differences can change token counts by up to 10-15% on some corpora, which matters for econ.
[06:42] Emma: On sample size, how many calls do you run to get stable p95?
[06:47] Anya: For tails we run sustained tests for at least 30 minutes under target concurrency, and repeated bursts (10x) to capture queuing effects. We'll also run a 24-hour soak if you want long-term stability. For POC we'll do a 2-4 hour representative suite and one extended soak if needed.
[07:06] Rajiv: One non-negotiable: encryption keys must be customer-controlled.
[07:10] Maya: KMS/HSM customer-managed keys supported in Private and via customer-managed KMS with Dedicated. We'll include configuration steps in the security appendix.
[07:19] Ben: Payment question — if we go Dedicated and commit, how quick is the cost break even?
[07:24] Anya: Depends on utilization. If you maintain >70% committed utilization, Dedicated reserved capacity typically gives 30-40% lower effective per-token cost compared to pay-as-you-go hosted. We'll model break-even in the spreadsheet for your expected RPS.
[07:40] Emma: For the bench, we'd like to see both latency and quality, and a combined cost-per-successful-query metric.
[07:46] Liam: We'll compute cost-per-successful-query by tying quality thresholds to outcomes; we'll include example thresholds and let you pick.
[07:56] Maya: Ok let's recap action items and timeline.
[08:00] Rajiv: Quick clarification — what exactly will you need from us to start infra?
[08:04] Liam: A VPC peering/connection diagram, a service account for deployment, and JIT access for our infra engineer. We'll detail the exact ports and SAML metadata in the email.
[08:17] Caroline: We'll coordinate the SAML and KMS leads internally.
[08:21] Maya: Great. We'll target a benchmark kickoff meeting (engineers only) the week of 2026-03-22. I'll send the scheduling poll.
[08:29] Ben: Sounds good. Any other questions?
[08:31] Emma: One last micro Q — do you support continuous KV cache invalidation? Our profiles change frequently.
[08:37] Liam: Yes, TTL-based invalidation plus manual invalidation APIs. We can also hash keys to namespace per-customer.
[08:46] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with SOW and security docs.
[08:50] Rajiv: Thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.

Notes: Imperfect ASR — occasional words mangled (e.g., "KV cash" in one snippet), speaker overlaps at times, punctuation is noisy. Bench numbers are estimates; final econ to be determined after benchmark runs.
